meta.blurb: A woman is attacked in a room with one locked door, one barred window and no chimney. Yet the attacker has vanished. Eighteen-year-old reporter Joseph Rouletabille says the answer is simple, if you take the puzzle by the right end.
meta.bible: Joseph Rouletabille: an eighteen-year-old reporter on the Epoque, round-headed, always smoking a pipe, who solves the case by taking his reason by the right end. Sainclair: his friend, a young lawyer, who tells the story. Professor Stangerson: a famous scientist who works on the Dissociation of Matter. Mathilde Stangerson: his daughter, aged thirty-five, who works with him. Robert Darzac: Mathilde's fiancé, a professor at the Sorbonne, who keeps a strange silence. Daddy Jacques: the old servant of the Stangersons, with a white beard and a Basque cap. Bernier: the gate-keeper, and his wife Madame Bernier, who poach rabbits. Frédéric Larsan: the famous detective of the Sûreté, also called Fred, who carries a yellow cane; in truth he is the criminal Ballmeyer. Monsieur de Marquet: the examining magistrate, who secretly writes plays. Monsieur Maleine: his registrar. Monsieur Dax: Chief of the Sûreté. Arthur Rance: an American from Philadelphia, a friend of the Stangersons, who drinks too much. The Green Man: the forest-keeper, handsome, dressed in green velvet. Daddy Mathieu: the bad-tempered landlord of the Donjon Inn. Madame Mathieu: his gentle wife. Mother Angenoux: an old woman of the forest, with a huge cat called the Bête du bon Dieu. Maître Henri Robert: Darzac's lawyer. Monsieur de Rocouz: the president of the court. The Yellow Room: Mathilde's small bedroom in the pavilion, with one door and one barred window. Château du Glandier: the old château in the forest near Epinay-sur-Orge, south of Paris. Paris. Versailles: where the trial is held. Philadelphia. Louisville. Cincinnati. America. Sorbonne. Élysée. The presbytery has lost nothing of its charm, nor the garden its brightness: the sentence that frightens Darzac and Mathilde. The perfume of the lady in black: Rouletabille's memory from childhood. Voice and tone: lively, clever and full of surprises, told by a friend who admires the young hero; the crime is stated plainly, without gore; the solution is simple and fair, and the secret is treated gently.

beats.scene: A lonely château stands in a dark forest near Paris
beats.summary: In October 1892 Paris learns that Mathilde Stangerson, daughter of a famous professor, has been attacked at the Château du Glandier.

beats.scene: Two men throw themselves against a locked door in a lamplit pavilion
beats.summary: Old Daddy Jacques tells how Mathilde locked and bolted herself into the Yellow Room at midnight, and how her cries and two shots were heard behind the door.

beats.scene: A wounded woman lies on the floor of a small yellow bedroom
beats.summary: When the door breaks open, Mathilde lies hurt among overturned furniture; the room holds a bloody handprint, a cap, a handkerchief, boot marks and a revolver, but no attacker.

beats.scene: A barred window and a bolted door in a small white pavilion
beats.summary: The only door was locked from inside, the one window barred, and there was no chimney; the magistrate says that otherwise one must believe in the Devil, and people whisper of a cat.

beats.scene: A round-headed young man waves a newspaper beside a bed
beats.summary: The eighteen-year-old reporter Joseph Rouletabille bursts in on his friend Sainclair, says the revolver was used by Mathilde, and takes him to the Glandier.

beats.scene: A young reporter and an elegant magistrate talk in a train compartment
beats.summary: On the train Rouletabille makes the magistrate talk; the wound was not made by the revolver, and the hall window has iron blinds, yet blood shows the murderer left that way.

beats.scene: Rouletabille stops a carriage at a park gate while a grey-haired detective watches
beats.summary: At the gate Rouletabille meets the detective Larsan and Mathilde's fiancé Darzac, who turns pale at a strange sentence about a presbytery and takes him in.

beats.scene: A young man kneels on the tiled floor of a small white hall
beats.summary: In the pavilion Rouletabille studies the hall, a drop of blood and the laboratory; Daddy Jacques says he washed the floors that afternoon and no boots had crossed them.

beats.scene: A young man in socks crawls under a bed in a small yellow room
beats.summary: Rouletabille crawls over the floor and searches walls, ceiling and window, finds no secret way, and declares that the Yellow Room was as tightly shut as an iron safe.

beats.scene: A pale woman speaks quietly to a magistrate and a clerk beside her bed
beats.summary: Mathilde tells the magistrate that she feared someone, borrowed Jacques's revolver, woke to find a man at her throat, fired at him, and remembers nothing after his blow.

beats.scene: Muddy footprints of heavy boots and neat boots run beside a marshy lake
beats.summary: Rouletabille follows the tracks to a lake where the heavy boot marks stop and neat prints and bicycle tracks begin, and insists the murderer had no accomplice.

beats.scene: Robert Darzac stares in horror at footprints beside a marshy lake
beats.summary: Larsan says the blood came from a nosebleed; Rouletabille warns him against fitting facts to an idea; then Darzac sees that the neat prints match his own feet.

beats.scene: A handsome man in green velvet walks past an old roadside inn
beats.summary: At the Donjon Inn Rouletabille says they will have to eat red meat now; the landlord Mathieu obeys and hisses that the forest-keeper in green is the murderer.

beats.scene: Officials and servants listen to a calm detective in a crowded laboratory
beats.summary: In the laboratory Larsan explains his theory that Professor Stangerson, alone at the door for a moment, let the murderer go to avoid a scandal.

beats.scene: The old professor raises his hand to swear while a young reporter bows
beats.summary: Stangerson swears by his daughter's head that the door never opened and that he does not know the murderer; everyone doubts him except Rouletabille.

beats.scene: The professor sits stunned before an empty iron cabinet
beats.summary: Rouletabille finds footprints and a parcel mark in the hall; the professor finds his iron cabinet empty, twenty years of work stolen, and only Mathilde kept the key.

beats.scene: A young reporter reads a small newspaper notice about a lost key
beats.summary: A notice about a lost bag with a brass key leads Rouletabille to the post office; a lady took a letter, and a man very like Darzac asked for it later.

beats.scene: A new yellow cane lies on a café table between two men
beats.summary: Rouletabille notices Larsan's new cane, said to come from London but marked by a Paris shop; Sainclair learns a man like Darzac bought it on the evening of the crime.

beats.scene: A woman in white and a man read a letter under a lamp
beats.summary: Rouletabille tells how at the Élysée reception he followed Mathilde into a garden and heard her read Darzac a letter ending with the presbytery sentence.

beats.scene: A telegram asks a young lawyer to come quickly and bring revolvers
beats.summary: On the second of November Rouletabille telegraphs Sainclair to come to the Glandier with revolvers, and says he expects the murderer that very evening.

beats.scene: A man in a stooping coat writes by candlelight at a lady's desk
beats.summary: Rouletabille tells how, on the night of the twenty-ninth of October, he found muddy footprints, climbed a ladder and saw a man writing at Mathilde's desk.

beats.scene: Three men wait at the ends of two long lamplit galleries
beats.summary: Rouletabille posts Larsan, Daddy Jacques and Stangerson at the ends of the galleries, climbs in and chases a red-bearded man out of Mathilde's room.

beats.scene: Four men stare at an empty gallery where a man has just vanished
beats.summary: At the crossing of the galleries the man is gone; they search everything, but every door and window is shut and nothing is hidden.

beats.scene: A pale woman in white stands at her door in her father's arms
beats.summary: Mathilde appears and says she slept in the boudoir with her nurses; the letter on her desk has gone; Rouletabille longs to save her without making her speak.

beats.scene: A young man traces a circle on his forehead while two keepers are freed
beats.summary: The forest-keeper says he saw no ladder; Rouletabille retreats to think within his circle of reason and has the poaching gate-keepers freed to be his helpers.

beats.scene: A worried man begs a young reporter to guard a lady through the night
beats.summary: Darzac asks Rouletabille to watch over Mathilde, saying he must go to Paris; he fears a new attack and will not name the murderer.

beats.scene: A woman pours drops from a small bottle into a glass
beats.summary: Rouletabille is sure the murderer will come, since Mathilde has sent her nurses away; at six he and Sainclair see her secretly drug her father's glass.

beats.scene: A detective collapses into an armchair at a dinner table
beats.summary: At dinner Larsan and Rouletabille each say they have found their man; then Larsan clutches his chest and falls into a deep sleep; Sainclair is sent to a dark closet.

beats.scene: A man in green carries a parcel along a lamplit gallery
beats.summary: From the dark closet Sainclair sees the forest-keeper leave Rance's room with a parcel and make signs from a window; nobody answers his signal and he finds Rouletabille asleep.

beats.scene: A man runs across a moonlit court as guns flash
beats.summary: Sainclair wakes Rouletabille; a death cry rings; a man flees Mathilde's rooms; shots are fired and Bernier's gun brings him down at the corner of the building.

beats.scene: A lantern lights the face of a dead man on stairs
beats.summary: The dead man is the forest-keeper, and Rouletabille shows that he was killed not by a bullet but by a knife thrust in the heart.

beats.scene: A wounded woman lies in bed while a man weeps beside her
beats.summary: Mathilde has been stabbed three times; the stolen papers lie on the floor; Darzac arrives at dawn crying that he is too late, and Rouletabille says she lives.

beats.scene: A magistrate arrests a pale professor as a woman cries from her bed
beats.summary: A railway worker saw Darzac at Epinay at half-past ten that night; he refuses to say why, and is arrested while Mathilde cries his name.

beats.scene: A young man with a travelling bag and an overcoat says goodbye
beats.summary: Rouletabille leaves on a long journey, having left his newspaper a sealed letter naming the murderer, to be opened in court if he is not back for Darzac's trial.

beats.scene: A great crowd presses at the steps of a courthouse at Versailles
beats.summary: On the fifteenth of January crowds flock to the court at Versailles; Darzac stays silent; Larsan gives his theory; the court waits for Rouletabille.

beats.scene: A young man in a travelling coat steps forward in a crowded courtroom
beats.summary: A young voice rings out from the back of the court: it is Rouletabille, who says he cannot name the murderer before half-past six.

beats.scene: A weeping woman nods as a young man speaks in court
beats.summary: Rouletabille explains that Madame Mathieu secretly met the keeper in the donjon at night, calling him with the cat's cry, and was the black phantom Daddy Jacques saw.

beats.scene: A young man points at an empty chair in a silent courtroom
beats.summary: At half-past six Rouletabille names Frédéric Larsan, who has left; he says Larsan is really Ballmeyer, a master criminal, and the court erupts.

beats.scene: A man climbs a wall to a terrace with an iron spike
beats.summary: Rouletabille shows an iron peg that fits a hole under the terrace; Larsan climbed to the gallery window while the others carried the keeper's body, and had drugged the reporter.

beats.scene: A young man explains how four men chased a fifth
beats.summary: Rouletabille explains the gallery mystery: the man could not have escaped, so one of the four pursuers was the murderer; in two seconds Larsan pulled off his false beard and joined the chase.

beats.scene: A pair of eye-glasses lies on a table in a young man's room
beats.summary: A pair of eye-glasses left in Mathilde's room proves Larsan was there; he loved her madly, found her lost key, stole the papers and returned them.

beats.scene: A bolted door of a small yellow room stands closed in the lamplight
beats.summary: Rouletabille announces that the murderer was never locked in the Yellow Room: the attack had happened hours earlier, at about six in the evening, when Mathilde went alone into her room.

beats.scene: A man waits under a bed as a woman enters her room
beats.summary: The murderer had hidden under the bed; when Mathilde came alone he seized her, she fired and wounded his hand, and he fled through the hall window, which she shut.

beats.scene: A woman sleeps in a locked room as a table falls
beats.summary: At midnight Mathilde, alone, dreams of the attack, cries out, overturns the table so that the revolver fires into the ceiling, and strikes her head on its marble corner.

beats.scene: Old boots, a worn cap and a handkerchief lie by a servant's door
beats.summary: Larsan had stolen Jacques's boots and cap and had boots made like Darzac's, to cast suspicion on both; as a detective he cleared one before accusing the other.

beats.scene: A free man leaves the courthouse among cheering crowds at night
beats.summary: The trial is adjourned; next day Darzac is freed and Jacques is cleared; Larsan cannot be found; Rouletabille becomes the hero of the hour.

beats.scene: Two friends ride a night train, one asleep by the window
beats.summary: On the train Rouletabille tells Sainclair how the lie about the cane should have warned them, and that Larsan bought it for his wounded hand; then he falls asleep.

beats.scene: A young woman in a lamplit drawing room listens to a charming Frenchman
beats.summary: The secret of Mathilde's past: in Philadelphia she loved a Frenchman called Jean Roussel, married him against her father's wish, and learned he was the criminal Ballmeyer.

beats.scene: A heartbroken young woman returns to her father's house
beats.summary: Mathilde returns to her father, hides the truth, believes Ballmeyer dead, agrees to marry Darzac, then the man reappears and threatens her in the name of their old house.

beats.scene: A thoughtful young reporter sits alone on a bench in a courthouse
beats.summary: Mathilde slowly recovers and Darzac is free; two months later Rouletabille sits sadly in the Palace of Justice, thinking of the perfume of the lady in black.

B1B2: In October 1892, the newspapers announce a frightful crime at the Château du Glandier, a lonely house in a forest near Paris. Mathilde Stangerson, the daughter of a famous scientist, has been attacked in her bedroom and is not expected to live.

At midnight, Mathilde says good night to her father and old Daddy Jacques, and locks and bolts herself into the Yellow Room. A few minutes later, they hear her cry for help and then two shots, but the door will not open.

When the door finally breaks open, Mathilde is lying on the floor with a terrible wound on her forehead. The room holds a bloody handprint, an old cap, a large handkerchief and the marks of heavy boots, but no attacker.

The room has only one door, locked from the inside, and one window with iron bars and closed shutters. The magistrate says that if no secret way is found, people will have to believe in the Devil, as Daddy Jacques says.

Joseph Rouletabille is only eighteen, but he is already the most gifted young reporter on the Epoque. He wakes his friend Sainclair, a young lawyer, and asks him to come to the Glandier and help him find the truth.

On the train to Epinay, Rouletabille cleverly makes the examining magistrate talk. The magistrate admits that the wound was not made by the revolver, and that blood on the hall window shows where the murderer left.

At the gate, Rouletabille meets the famous detective Frédéric Larsan and Mathilde's fiancé, Robert Darzac. When he says a mysterious sentence about a presbytery and a garden, Darzac turns pale and takes him inside.

The pavilion has a hall, a laboratory and the Yellow Room, and Rouletabille studies every corner of it. Daddy Jacques says that he washed the floors that very afternoon, and that no boots had crossed them.
In his socks, Rouletabille crawls under the bed and measures every wall, the ceiling and the window bars. At last he says that the Yellow Room was as tightly shut as an iron safe.

Mathilde, a little stronger, tells the magistrate that she had felt afraid for several nights and had borrowed Daddy Jacques's revolver. She woke to find a man attacking her, fired at him, and remembers nothing after his blow.

Rouletabille follows the footprints to a pond, where the marks of heavy boots stop and the prints of neat boots begin. He explains that there was no accomplice, only one man who changed his boots and walked his bicycle to the road.

Larsan says that the murderer's blood came from a nosebleed, but Rouletabille warns him not to fit the facts to his own idea. Then Rouletabille sees that Robert Darzac's footprints are exactly like the neat ones, and Darzac turns white with fear.

At the Donjon Inn, Rouletabille says a strange sentence about red meat, and the angry innkeeper, Daddy Mathieu, suddenly becomes helpful. When the forest-keeper, a handsome man dressed in green, walks past, Mathieu says that he is the murderer.

The magistrate and the chief of the police gather everyone in the laboratory, and Larsan explains how the murderer could have left the room. He believes that Professor Stangerson, alone at the door for a moment, let the man go to avoid a scandal.

Professor Stangerson swears, by the head of his suffering daughter, that the door never opened and that he does not know the murderer. Everyone doubts him except Rouletabille, who shakes his hand and says, “I believe you.”

Rouletabille shows that a thief had also been in the hall, and the professor discovers that his iron cabinet is empty. Twenty years of work by father and daughter have disappeared, and only Mathilde ever carried the little key.

Rouletabille has read a small advertisement about a lost bag with a brass-headed key, signed with the initials of Mathilde Stangerson. At the post office he learned that a lady had taken the letter, and that a man like Darzac had asked for it later.

Rouletabille notices that Larsan carries a new yellow cane, which he says came from London but bears the name of a Paris shop. Sainclair learns that a man like Darzac bought it on the evening of the crime.

Rouletabille explains that the night before the crime he followed Mathilde and Darzac into a garden at a great reception. There he heard Mathilde read a letter that ended with the strange sentence, and Darzac ask whether he must commit a crime to win her.

On the second of November, Sainclair receives a telegram from Rouletabille asking him to come to the Glandier and bring revolvers. At the château, the young reporter tells him calmly that he expects the murderer that very evening.

Rouletabille tells how, a few nights before, he heard the strange cry of the cat and found muddy footprints in the gallery of the château. Climbing a ladder, he looked into Mathilde's room and saw a man with his back to him, writing at her desk.

Rouletabille wakes Larsan and Stangerson and places them and Daddy Jacques at the ends of the two galleries so that nobody can escape. Then he climbs in through the window and chases a red-bearded man out of Mathilde's room.

The four men rush together at the crossing of the galleries, but the man is not there. Larsan says he touched him and Daddy Jacques felt his breath, yet every door and window is locked and nothing is hidden.

Mathilde appears at her door in a white dressing-gown and says that she slept that night in the next room with her nurses. The letter that had been on her desk has disappeared, and Rouletabille longs to save her without making her speak.

The forest-keeper, found awake and angry, says he saw no ladder, and Rouletabille retreats to think. He also has the two gate-keepers set free, because they were only poaching rabbits on the night of the crime.

Before leaving for Paris, Robert Darzac begs Rouletabille to watch over Mathilde all night, because he fears a new attack when he is away. He does not say why he cannot stay, and he will not give the name of the murderer.

Rouletabille is sure that the murderer will come that night, because Mathilde has sent her nurses away for twenty-four hours. Then he and Sainclair see her secretly pour the contents of a small bottle into her father's glass.

Rouletabille, Sainclair and Larsan dine together, and the two rivals agree that each has found his criminal and that it will be a fight. Suddenly Larsan clutches his chest and falls into a deep sleep, as if he had been drugged.

From his dark hiding place, Sainclair watches the forest-keeper leave Arthur Rance's room with a large package and make signs from a window. He gives the agreed signal, but nobody comes, and half an hour later he finds Rouletabille asleep on the floor.

Sainclair throws cold water on Rouletabille's face, and a terrible cry rings through the house. They see a man run from Mathilde's rooms, fire at him, and watch Bernier's gun bring him down at the corner.
By the light of a lantern they see that the dead man is the forest-keeper. Rouletabille opens his coat and shows that he did not die of a bullet at all, but of a knife thrust in the heart.
Mathilde has been wounded three times by a knife and lies between life and death. Darzac arrives at dawn, crying that he is too late, and Rouletabille answers that she lives.
A railway worker says that he saw Darzac at the village station at half-past ten that night, but Darzac will not say why. The magistrate arrests him, and Mathilde cries out his name from her bed.

The next morning Rouletabille says goodbye to Sainclair and says he will be away for a month or two. He has left his newspaper a sealed letter naming the murderer, to be read in court if he is not back in time.

On the fifteenth of January, great crowds hurry to the court at Versailles, where Robert Darzac stands trial for the crime. Darzac refuses to explain where he was that night, and the court waits in vain for Rouletabille.

As Larsan finishes, a youthful voice cries from the back of the court, “It is I, Monsieur President—Joseph Rouletabille.” The crowd laughs with relief, and the young man says that he cannot name the murderer before half-past six.

Rouletabille explains that Madame Mathieu used to meet the forest-keeper at night in the old tower, calling him with the cry of the cat. She was the black phantom that Daddy Jacques saw, and he had kept her secret out of pity.

At half-past six Rouletabille declares that Frédéric Larsan is the murderer, and the usher reports that Larsan left the court at four o'clock. Larsan is really Ballmeyer, a master criminal whom the police have hunted for years.

Rouletabille shows an iron peg that fits a hole under the terrace, where Larsan climbed up to the gallery window. While the others carried the keeper's body, the detective went into his room and called out as if he had just woken.

Rouletabille explains the gallery mystery: nobody could have escaped, so one of the four men chasing the murderer must have been the murderer himself. During the two seconds when Rouletabille lost sight of him, Larsan pulled off his false beard and joined the chase.

Rouletabille shows the eye-glasses that Larsan left in Mathilde's room, and says that the detective was a man who loved her madly. He had found her lost bag and used its key to take her father's papers, which he returned on the night of the keeper's death.

Rouletabille says that the murderer did not need to escape from the Yellow Room, because he was not in it at midnight. The attack had happened earlier, in the evening, when Mathilde went to her room alone for a moment.

The murderer was hiding in the pavilion when Mathilde came into her room alone, and he seized her by the throat. She fired and wounded his hand, and he dropped his weapon and escaped through the hall window.

At midnight Mathilde, alone in the locked room, dreams that the murderer is attacking her again and cries for help. She knocks over the table, the revolver falls and fires into the ceiling, and she hits her head on the table.

Larsan had stolen Daddy Jacques's old boots and cap, and had boots made like Darzac's, so that suspicion would fall on both men. As a famous detective, he proved one innocent first and then accused the other, a trick he had used before.
The court adjourns, and the next day Darzac is freed and Daddy Jacques is cleared. Larsan is hunted everywhere, but he has vanished, and the crowd carries Rouletabille through the streets in triumph.

On the train home, Rouletabille tells Sainclair how Larsan's lie about the cane should have warned them. He explains that the detective bought it to carry in his wounded hand, and then he falls asleep in mid-sentence.

Years earlier, in Philadelphia, young Mathilde had fallen in love with a charming Frenchman called Jean Roussel, and her father had forbidden the marriage. She ran away and married him in secret, but she soon learned that her husband was really the criminal Ballmeyer.

Mathilde went home to her father and hid the truth, and later she believed that Ballmeyer was dead. Years later, when she agreed to marry Darzac, he came back into her life and wrote to her about the presbytery.

Mathilde is slowly getting better and Darzac is free, but two months later Rouletabille sits sadly on a bench in the courthouse. He says that he is thinking of the perfume of the lady in black, and that perhaps he will tell that story some day.
C1C2: On the twenty-fifth of October 1892, an evening paper reported a frightful crime at the Château du Glandier, the lonely house in the forest where Professor Stangerson carried out his famous experiments. His daughter and fellow worker, Mathilde, had been attacked in the night, and the doctors would not promise that she would live. Paris, which followed the labours of father and daughter with admiration, was gripped by the news, and nobody guessed that it would prove the strangest riddle in the history of crime.

At midnight Mathilde kissed her father, wished good night to the old servant Daddy Jacques, and went into her little bedroom, which people called the Yellow Room, where she turned the key and shot the bolt. Half an hour later her voice broke out in a desperate cry for help, followed by the sound of two shots and of furniture crashing to the floor. The two men threw themselves against the door, but it was locked on the inside, and it held firm while the cries grew weaker and then stopped.

When the door gave way at last, the lamp showed Mathilde lying in her nightdress among overturned furniture, with marks on her throat and a wound on her temple, but she was still breathing. The little room held the print of a large red hand on the wall, a bloodstained handkerchief, an old cap, fresh marks of heavy boots, an enormous bone, and Daddy Jacques's own revolver. The attacker, however, had vanished, for nobody was under the bed or behind the furniture, and the four people who had burst in swore that he had not passed them.

The Yellow Room was very small, yet the more the police studied it, the stranger it seemed, for its only door had been locked from within, its one window was barred, and it had no chimney. The examining magistrate, Monsieur de Marquet, admitted that he had never known such a case, and said that unless a builder's pickaxe found a secret passage, one must really believe in the Devil. In the forest, meanwhile, people whispered about the huge cat of old Mother Angenoux, which they called the Bête du bon Dieu, and whose mournful cry had been heard that night.

Joseph Rouletabille, a round-headed young reporter of eighteen who was never without his pipe, burst into the bedroom of his friend Sainclair, the lawyer who tells this story, waving the morning paper. He declared that the crime was the strangest in years, and that in his opinion the revolver had been used not by the murderer but by Mademoiselle Stangerson herself, who had wounded the man. Then he asked Sainclair to dress quickly and come with him to the Château du Glandier, because the Epoque had trusted him with the case, and he meant to solve it.

Rouletabille slipped into the train compartment of the examining magistrate and, by pretending to be a theatre critic, soon had him talking about his secret hobby of writing plays. Little by little the magistrate let slip that Mathilde's wound had not been made by the revolver, and that the only unbarred window, in the entrance hall, had iron blinds that were still fastened. Rouletabille then asked how Mathilde had worn her hair that night, and he sighed with disappointment when he heard that it had been drawn back from her forehead.

At the park gate Rouletabille greeted the famous detective Frédéric Larsan, whom the Sûreté called the great Fred, and then he stopped the carriage of Mathilde's fiancé, Robert Darzac, who was hurrying to the station. Then he repeated a strange sentence, that the presbytery had lost nothing of its charm, nor the garden its brightness, and at those words the professor from the Sorbonne turned pale. Darzac climbed down from his carriage, begged the young reporter to come in, and from that moment he helped him in every way, as if he dared refuse him nothing.

The pavilion, a white building that looked like a tomb in the oak grove, had a small hall with an unbarred window, a large laboratory with barred windows, and the Yellow Room, which opened only into the laboratory. Rouletabille went down on his knees to examine the hall, found a drop of blood, and noted that the murderer's heavy boots had left their black marks in the bedroom but not on the freshly washed floor outside it. Daddy Jacques, who had scrubbed the tiles that very afternoon, could only repeat that nobody could have walked across the hall without leaving a trace.

Rouletabille slipped into the Yellow Room in his socks and crept under the bed, where he found the marks of hobnails, and then he examined the walls, the ceiling and the hole made by the second bullet. He climbed on a table to touch the plaster, shook the bars of the window, and even found a woman's blond hair, which he folded carefully into a piece of paper. When he finally came out, perspiring, he declared that the Yellow Room had been as tightly shut as an iron safe.

While Rouletabille waited downstairs, the magistrate questioned Mathilde in her room, and she told him quietly that for several nights she had heard footsteps and seen shadows near the pavilion, so that she had secretly taken Daddy Jacques's revolver. She had locked herself in, gone to sleep, and woken to find a man at her throat, and she had snatched the revolver from her night table and fired just as he lifted a heavy weapon over her head. Then came the blow, and she knew nothing more, not even whether the man was tall or short, for she had seen only a formidable shadow.

The tracks led across the park to a small, marshy lake where the great detective Larsan was prodding the mud with his cane, and there the marks of the heavy boots suddenly disappeared. Beside them Rouletabille found the neat prints of a different pair and the light tracks of a bicycle, and he reasoned that the murderer had changed his boots. There had been no accomplice, he insisted, and Larsan, smiling coldly, answered that they were both reaching the same conclusion.

Larsan insisted that the murderer had not been wounded at all, since the red drops on the floor and the handkerchief came from a nosebleed, and Rouletabille replied that the detective was twisting logic to suit his idea. He warned the great Fred that it is dangerous to go from a fixed idea to the proofs that fit it, and then he danced with delight at the thought of beating him. Suddenly he stopped, for Robert Darzac was staring at the neat footprints beside his own, and there was not a particle of difference between them.

The Donjon Inn was an old roadside house where the landlord, Daddy Mathieu, claimed to have no food, until Rouletabille remarked that they would have to eat red meat now, and the man at once changed his manner. While they cooked an omelette on the fire, a handsome man in green velvet, with a gun on his back and glasses on his nose, passed along the road, and the landlord shook with hatred. This was the forest-keeper of the Glandier, and after he had left, Mathieu hissed that he was the man who had tried to murder Mademoiselle Stangerson.

The magistrate gathered the professor, Darzac, Daddy Jacques, the concierges and the Chief of the Sûreté in the laboratory, where Larsan threw down a pair of muddy boots that Daddy Jacques knew as his own. Then he explained the escape, saying that during the moments when the professor stood alone before the door, the murderer had walked out, and that Stangerson, for reasons of his own, had let him go. It was a cruel suggestion, for it meant that the father had left his daughter to die behind a locked door in order to protect some terrible secret.

The old professor rose, as pale as a statue, and swore by the head of his suffering child that the door had never been opened and that he did not know the murderer. The listeners did not believe him, for Larsan's cold logic seemed to leave no other answer. Only Rouletabille walked up to him, took his hand with great respect, and said quietly that he believed him.

Kneeling in the hall, Rouletabille pointed to two footprints and the mark of a heavy parcel in the dust, which showed that a thief had gathered something to carry away. At that moment a cry came from the laboratory, where the professor had opened his iron cabinet and found it empty. Twenty years of experiments by father and daughter had vanished, and the only key, a small one with a brass head, had always been in the keeping of Mathilde.

A few days before the crime, Rouletabille explained, a small newspaper notice had offered a reward for a lost black bag that held a key with a brass head. The initials at the bottom suggested Mathilde Stangerson, and at the post office he learned that a lady had collected a letter, and that the next day a man very like Robert Darzac had asked for it. Since Mathilde had lost her bag in a shop while Darzac stood beside her, suspicion began to fall more and more heavily upon her fiancé.

Rouletabille had noticed that the great Fred, who had never carried a stick before, now never let go of a new yellow bamboo cane, and he asked him where he had found it. Larsan answered calmly that it had been given to him in London, but when Rouletabille read out the name of a Paris shop on the handle, the detective only shrugged his shoulders. That evening Sainclair visited the shop and learned that a man who looked exactly like Robert Darzac had bought a cane of that kind at eight o'clock on the night of the crime.

On the night before the crime, Rouletabille said, he had followed a lady in white through a great reception at the Élysée, because her perfume reminded him of a lady in black from his childhood. She was Mathilde Stangerson, and in the dark garden he heard her read to Robert Darzac a letter that ended with the sentence about the presbytery. Darzac asked in a trembling voice whether he must commit a crime to win her, and afterwards he begged Rouletabille never to repeat what he had heard.

A week after these events, on the second of November, Sainclair received a telegram that said, “Come to the Glandier by the earliest train, and bring revolvers.” He bought a good pistol for his friend, hurried to the station, and found Rouletabille on the doorstep of the château, in excellent spirits though the situation was going badly. Larsan was working against Darzac with all his might, said the young man, and that very evening he expected the murderer to come again.

Rouletabille told how, on the night of the twenty-ninth of October, he had woken to the sad cry of the Bête du bon Dieu and found muddy footprints on the carpet of the gallery, leading to Mathilde's rooms. With Daddy Jacques's help he set a ladder against her window, and through a gap in the blinds he saw a man with a stooping back writing by candlelight at her desk. Mathilde was not in the room, and Rouletabille decided not to spring in at once but to prepare a trap.

He woke Frédéric Larsan and Professor Stangerson, and, with Daddy Jacques, he posted them at the ends of the two galleries that met near Mathilde's door, so that the man would have to run straight into them. Then he climbed the ladder again and sprang through the window just as the man, with long red hair and a great red beard, leapt up, flung open the door, and fled. Rouletabille ran after him down the gallery, shouting for help, and he reached the meeting-point of the galleries less than two seconds behind the man.

The four men ran together to the crossing of the two galleries, and the man was not there. Larsan cried that he had touched him and Daddy Jacques that he had felt his breath on his face, yet they searched every corner, door and window in a frenzy and found all of them tightly closed. The gallery was brightly lit, with neither secret door nor hiding place, and Rouletabille confessed that for a moment he felt done for, since the man seemed to have melted into the air.

Mathilde Stangerson appeared at the door of her ante-room, wholly in white and very pale, and her father took her in his arms and kissed her as if he had recovered her after a long loss. She explained that she had slept that night in the little boudoir with her nurses, and Rouletabille noticed that the letter which had lain on her desk was no longer there. As he looked at her, he felt more strongly than ever that she knew the murderer and that she would sooner die than name him, and he swore silently to save her without forcing her to speak.

Larsan and Rouletabille went down to the little room where the forest-keeper slept, but the man put them out, saying that he had seen no ladder and wanted to go to bed. Rouletabille spent the following day walking about the gallery, and he told himself that he had drawn a circle of reason between the two bumps on his forehead and that the truth had to lie inside it. He had also persuaded the professor to sign a promise to keep the gate-keepers, who confessed that they were only poaching rabbits that night, and, being freed and grateful, they became his helpers.

On the evening before, Darzac had knocked at Rouletabille's door and confessed, in a broken voice, that he had to go to Paris the next morning and could not say why. He feared that Mathilde would be attacked again while he was away, since both earlier attacks had happened on nights when some strange duty kept him from her side. When Rouletabille asked him to name the murderer, he grew pale and answered that he could not know such a thing, but the young man saw that he was guarding a secret that he would die rather than tell.

Rouletabille was certain that the man would come that night, for at half-past ten that morning he had learned that Mathilde had found excuses to send her nurses away for twenty-four hours. As the two friends passed her open door at six o'clock, they saw her take advantage of the steward's absence to pour the contents of a small bottle into her father's glass while he stooped to pick something up. Rouletabille understood that she meant to send her father to sleep so that nobody would disturb her meeting with the murderer.

The three men dined in Larsan's room and spoke carefully, and each said that he had found his criminal, Rouletabille declaring that Darzac was an honest man and Larsan that he was nothing of the kind. A moment later Larsan pressed both hands to his chest, cried out that he had been poisoned, and sank into an armchair in a heavy sleep. Rouletabille declared calmly that he was only asleep, and at ten o'clock he told Sainclair to cock his revolver and sent him alone to a dark closet in the gallery, where he was to watch.

Sainclair waited in the dark closet for more than an hour, until, at half-past eleven, three sharp cries of the Bête du bon Dieu rose from the park and the door of Arthur Rance's room opened. Out came the forest-keeper in his green clothes, carrying a bulky parcel, and after making two signs from a window he went down the stairs, so that Sainclair released the curtain cord as agreed. Nobody appeared, however, and after half an hour of silence he crept to Rouletabille's room and found his friend stretched on the floor in a heavy sleep.

Sainclair threw a jug of cold water over his friend and shook him until he stood up, and at that moment a terrible cry, a veritable death cry, rang through the château. He ran along the gallery with his revolver, saw a man hurrying away from Mathilde's door, and fired, then chased him down the stairs and out of a window with Arthur Rance, who fired his own revolver too. Above their heads Rouletabille shouted to Bernier, the gate-keeper, to fire, and at the flash of his gun the fleeing shadow fell dead at the corner of the building.

They carried the body into the vestibule, and, by the light of Daddy Jacques's lantern, they recognised the forest-keeper whom the landlord of the Donjon Inn had called the Green Man. Daddy Jacques wept as if for his own son, and the others could only stare, because Larsan and Rouletabille had both hoped for a very different result. Then Rouletabille laid bare the dead man's chest and announced, in a voice full of savage irony, that the man they believed they had shot had been killed by a knife thrust in the heart.

Rouletabille staggered to Mathilde's room, where he found her lying over her desk with three knife wounds in her breast, and with the help of her half-drugged father he carried her to her bed. Beside the desk lay the large parcel of the stolen papers, returned by the murderer in the very hour he tried to kill her. When Darzac rushed in at half-past nine, white and wild, crying that he had come too late, Rouletabille told him that she was still alive, though her mind was badly shaken.

Larsan returned with a young railway employee who swore that he had seen Robert Darzac step off the train at Epinay-sur-Orge at half-past ten on the night of the crime. The magistrate demanded to know how Darzac had spent his time, and when Darzac refused to answer, he arrested him in the name of the law, with tears in many eyes. From her bed, Mathilde cried out his name in despair, and Rouletabille whispered to the prisoner that he would defend him, because he knew more than Darzac did.

The next morning Rouletabille appeared at Sainclair's rooms with a valise in his hand and announced that he would be away for a month or two. He had left at the newspaper a sealed letter naming the murderer, to be opened in court on the day of Darzac's trial if he himself had not returned. For two months nobody heard anything from him, and on the fifteenth of January the whole of France waited to see whether the young reporter would keep his promise.

On the fifteenth of January crowds fought for places at the Assize Court of Versailles, for the newspaper had promised that it possessed the truth and that Joseph Rouletabille would explain everything, or that his letter would be read. Robert Darzac stood calm and handsome in the dock, but when the president told him that his silence about his movements might cost him his life, he answered quietly that he would submit to it, for he was innocent. Larsan, meanwhile, gave the court his own clear theory, that the man who attacked Mathilde had also killed the keeper, and the clock moved on while the court waited for the young reporter.

As Larsan finished speaking, a clear young voice rang out from the back of the court, saying that it agreed with Larsan about the death of the keeper but not about the escape of the murderer. The president angrily ordered the intruder to be thrown out, until the voice replied that it was Joseph Rouletabille, and the whole court broke into cheers. He stepped into the witness box with his overcoat on his arm, said that he had come straight from America, and added calmly that he could not give the murderer's name before half-past six o'clock.

He told the court that Madame Mathieu had been secretly meeting the forest-keeper at night in an old room of the donjon, and that she called her friend by imitating the cry of Mother Angenoux's cat. Daddy Jacques, who knew that the black phantom he had seen in the park was only this woman, had kindly led her to the road and later hidden the whole matter to protect her name. Madame Mathieu, weeping, admitted that it had all happened exactly as the young man described, as if he had been walking behind her.

At half-past six the court fell silent as Rouletabille announced that the murderer had been in the courtyard of the château on the night of the keeper's death, leaning from a window above. Then he named Frédéric Larsan, and when the usher returned with the news that the detective had left at four o'clock and had not been seen since, Rouletabille cried that this was his proof. Larsan, he declared, was the notorious Ballmeyer, a master swindler and criminal who for twenty years had eluded the police of two continents, and the court broke into uproar.

The murderer, said Rouletabille, had climbed to the terrace while everyone was busy with the keeper's body, using an iron peg that he had driven into the cornice beforehand and that fitted a hole still visible there. He had then entered the gallery through the window and called out to the others as if he had just woken, for a man of Ballmeyer's strength found such a feat child's play. His pretended sleep at dinner had been acting, because it was he who had drugged Rouletabille, hoping to reach Mathilde's room without being watched.

Since the man could not have escaped from the gallery by any door or window, Rouletabille reasoned, he had never left it, and the only people there besides the murderer were Stangerson, Daddy Jacques, Larsan and himself. He had seen the murderer at the same moment as each of the others, but never at the same moment as Larsan. In the two seconds when the man had been out of sight, the detective had time to pull off his false beard and run back to join the pursuers.

The eye-glasses, Rouletabille told the court, had been left in Mathilde's room by Larsan, who had risked a second visit to look for them because they would have shown that he was long-sighted. He had gone there, the young man believed, because he loved Mathilde madly and wished to prevent her marriage to Darzac, and for that reason he had picked up her lost bag and learned about the brass key. Having stolen the papers from the iron cabinet, and finding them of no use, he returned them on the night of the keeper's death, hoping perhaps to win her gratitude.

The Yellow Room, said Rouletabille, had been closed like a safe from the moment Mathilde locked herself in until the door was broken, so the murderer had not been in it during that time. The marks he had left, the cap, the handkerchief, the bloody hand and the boots, had been made hours earlier and simply left behind. The attack had really happened about six in the evening, when Mathilde went alone into her room, and what the others heard at midnight was a second, quite different scene.

The man had entered the pavilion by the hall window while Mathilde and her father were out walking, and he had hidden under the bed, waiting for a moment when she would be alone. When she came into her room, he seized her by the throat, but she snatched the revolver from her night table and fired, wounding the hand that held the bone with which he meant to strike her. He dropped it, staggered against the wall, leaving the red print of his hand, and fled through the hall window, which Mathilde hurried to shut before she returned to her father as if nothing had happened.

Mathilde, who had forgotten that the traces of the first struggle were still in her room, went to bed at midnight, worn out with fear, and in her nightmare she saw the murderer spring upon her again. She cried out for help, and her hand, seeking the revolver, overturned the little table, so that the weapon fell to the floor and went off, sending its bullet into the ceiling. As she rose from her bed she fell heavily and struck her temple on the corner of the marble table top, and Rouletabille had found there a blond hair stained with blood to prove it.

Larsan, who had visited the pavilion before the crime disguised as a messenger from the Sûreté, had stolen from Daddy Jacques a pair of old boots and a worn cap. He had left them where they would cast suspicion on the old servant, and he had also had boots made to match the neat prints of Darzac, whom he hated and wished to see ruined. As a detective he had even cleared Jacques before accusing Darzac, a clever trick that had hidden his guilt in other cases, which Rouletabille said must now be reviewed.

Rouletabille's speech was greeted with a storm of applause, and the lawyer for the defence asked for an adjournment, which the public prosecutor himself supported. On the following day Robert Darzac was released on bail and Daddy Jacques was cleared, while the police searched everywhere for Frédéric Larsan and found no trace of him. Rouletabille became the hero of the hour, and when he left the court the crowd bore him shoulder-high, though success did not turn his head.

On the train home from Versailles, Sainclair pressed his friend with questions, and Rouletabille admitted that Larsan's lie about the cane, which he said had been given to him in London, should have warned them long before. Larsan had bought it at eight o'clock that same evening, he explained, straight after the first attack, because Mathilde's bullet had wounded his hand and the cane helped him to hide the injury. He had even noticed a thin silk bandage on the hand at the dinner, but it was too late then, and a moment later the young man was fast asleep with his head against the window.

The secret of Mathilde Stangerson, which could now be told, began long before, in Philadelphia, where she had lived with her father as a girl and had fallen in love with a witty, graceful Frenchman who called himself Jean Roussel. When Monsieur Stangerson discovered that the man was a swindler and refused his consent, the young woman, indignant, ran away to be married, and the couple lived for some time in Louisville. One morning the police knocked at their door to arrest Roussel, and she learned that her husband was in truth the notorious Ballmeyer.

Heart-broken, Mathilde returned to her father, who never knew where she had been, and when a rumour said that Ballmeyer was dead she devoted herself to her work, believing that she had atoned for her disobedience. When at last she agreed to marry Robert Darzac, to whom she told everything, the man she thought dead reappeared and wrote to her that the presbytery had lost nothing of its charm. That was the name of the little house in Louisville where they had lived, and he threatened to destroy her father's life work, so she hid the horrible truth rather than let the old professor know.

Mathilde slowly recovered, and Robert Darzac, free and happy again, hoped that careful nursing would one day give her back her peace of mind. The mystery of the Yellow Room had been solved by a boy of eighteen, who had followed reason to the end and still protected the secret that had cost her so dearly. Two months later Sainclair found his friend alone on a bench in the Palace of Justice, looking sad, and Rouletabille would only sigh that he was thinking of the perfume of the lady in black.
